sources.quote: Allow sufficient space for ultimate width of hedge when established, 450—1 200.
sources.value: hedge ultimate width 450-1200 mm
sources.note: Applies to: clipped/flowering garden hedges. Temperate-climate (northern Europe/US) practice; hedge species choice for Egypt needs local data. Also says plant hedges for protection from cold N and E winds (NH temperate; not applicable to Egypt winter/dust logic).

sources.document: Neufert, Architects' Data
sources.quote: Allow 600—1 000 depth for planting trees, 500 for climbers and wall plants, 300 for shrub beds, 150 for grassed areas.
sources.value: topsoil depth: trees 600-1000, climbers 500, shrub beds 300, lawn 150 mm
sources.note: In-ground depths; a different context from planting over structure (TS 610-4), which LS-SOIL-DEPTH uses. Applies to: planting beds and lawn. Soil-depth figures; relevant to desert/fill soils (import topsoil). Climate-neutral.

sources.document: Neufert, Architects' Data
sources.quote: Depth water not less than 355 so that water lilies may be planted in boxes for ease of removal.
sources.value: min water depth 355 mm (lily/fish pool); built-in concrete shell 127-152 mm thick
sources.note: A water-lily pool floor, not a koi depth; no rule uses it. Applies to: ornamental water-lily and fish pools. Not a koi-specific depth (koi need ~1.0-1.5 m, not in Neufert). Also states pools sited for max sun: conflicts with Egyptian heat and algae/evaporation, shade is needed. Provide overflow pipe and removable drain plug.

sources.document: Neufert, Architects' Data
sources.quote: No deciduous trees or shrubs by pool to avoid leaves dropping
sources.value: no deciduous trees/shrubs adjacent to pool
sources.note: Swimming-pool siting; used only as a second voice for the leaf-fall advisory. Applies to: garden pool siting; also pool close to kitchen/living room within sight (children). Siting rule applicable to koi pond (leaf fall, water quality) and supervision. Climate-neutral.

sources.document: Neufert, Architects' Data
sources.quote: Built-in barbecues a ad justable grill can be raised to 305 above brazier on masonry base
sources.value: grill adjustable to 305 mm above brazier; barbecue/firepit combination continuous with garden seat and patio paving; hard-burned firebrick liner
sources.note: Applies to: built-in barbecue/firepit combination. US design examples; no clearance-to-building/fence distance given. No fire-pit setback found in Neufert.

sources.document: Buxton (ed.), Metric Handbook: Planning and Design Data
sources.quote: is 0.75 m2 per audience member for seated audiences, but this can range from 0.6 m2 per audience member where audience members would be tightly packed in to 1.5 m2 for generously provided foyer spaces with lounge areas
sources.value: 0.6 (tight) / 0.75 (typical) / 1.5 m2 per person (generous with lounge areas)
sources.note: Foyer with lounge areas in a theatre; borrowed context. Applies to: auditorium foyer gathering space incl. lounge areas. Theatre foyer, not garden; useful as a generous-gathering-with-lounge density. Climate-neutral.

sources.document: Buxton (ed.), Metric Handbook: Planning and Design Data
sources.quote: Floor space factors for calculating the recommended maximum numbers of people permitted within a given area without overcrowding
sources.value: Standing area for spectators 0.3 m2/person; bars without seating 0.3 m2/person; dance area 0.5 m2/person; restaurant tables around dance area 1.0-1.5 m2; exhibition spaces 1.5 m2; art galleries 5.0 m2 (table read from rendered page; text extraction separates rows from values)
sources.note: Crowd-safety MAXIMUM densities (0.3 m2 standing), not comfort areas. No rule uses it (a test asserts this). Values read from the rendered table. Applies to: maximum safe crowd capacity (UK entertainment venues). Maximum-capacity / crowd-safety figures, NOT comfort. A standing reception at ease is much looser; do not use 0.3 for a garden party.

sources.document: Mitton & Nystuen, Residential Interior Design
sources.quote: groups larger than six tend to splinter into smaller conversations
sources.value: seating group max 6 people; divide a larger space into several clusters
sources.note: Applies to: social/leisure seating areas (10-20 guests = 2-4 clusters). Observed design rule, US residential. Climate-neutral.

sources.document: Mitton & Nystuen, Residential Interior Design
sources.quote: the actual area of a conversation cluster should be approximately 12 to 13 feet (3,658 to 3,962 mm) in diameter to best support interaction
sources.value: 12-13 ft (3.66-3.96 m) diameter per conversation cluster (4 to 6 people); face-to-face limit 6-10 ft (1.2-3.0 m)
sources.note: Applies to: indoor lounge/conversation seating groups; transferable to an outdoor lounge cluster. Indoor US residential guidance; seating-group dimension, not a m2/person figure. Climate-neutral.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Similar to the manner in which a shade tree offers a sense of enclosure beneath its umbrella structure, an overhead plane defines a field of space between itself and the ground plane.
sources.value: Does anything overhead (canopy, pergola, tree crown) give this spot a defined, roofed field, and are its edges and height set deliberately?
sources.note: Building-focused chapter; the tree analogy is the only planting reference.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Since the edges of the overhead plane establish the boundaries of this field, its shape, size, and height above the ground plane determines the formal qualities of the space.
sources.value: What are the shape, size and height of the overhead element, and do they set the quality of the space beneath?
sources.note: General space theory, not garden-specific.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The surface articulation of the ground or floor plane is often used in architecture to define a zone of space within a larger context.
sources.value: Is the ground surface (paving, lawn, gravel) used to mark out a distinct zone within the larger garden?
sources.note: Needs a perceptible change in colour, tone or texture to work (same page).

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: For a horizontal plane to be seen as a figure, there must be a perceptible change in color, tone, or texture between its surface and that of the surrounding area.
sources.value: Is the contrast between this surface and its surround strong enough for the zone to read as a figure?
sources.note: Qualitative; no threshold given.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: When 2 feet high, a plane defines the edge of a spatial field but provides little or no sense of enclosure. When waist-high, it begins to provide a sense of enclosure while allowing for visual continuity with the adjoining space.
sources.value: At the planned wall/hedge height, how much enclosure versus continuity does the boundary give?
sources.note: Heights are illustrative anchors (2 ft, waist, eye level), not a design standard.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: When it approaches our eye level in height, it begins to separate one space from another. Above our height, a plane interrupts the visual and spatial continuity between two fields and provides a strong sense of enclosure.
sources.value: Does the boundary reach eye level or above, and is that separation intended?
sources.note: Same caveat: qualitative degrees.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Vertical forms have a greater presence in our visual field than horizontal planes and are therefore more instrumental in defining a discrete volume of space and providing a sense of enclosure and privacy for those within it.
sources.value: Are the vertical elements (walls, hedges, screens) doing the real work of enclosure and privacy, rather than the ground plane alone?
sources.note: Written for buildings.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The linear members of trellises and pergolas can provide a moderate degree of definition and enclosure for outdoor spaces while allowing filtered sunlight and breezes to penetrate.
sources.value: Would a trellis or pergola give partial enclosure here while keeping light and air?
sources.note: Says nothing about climbers or planting.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.locator: p. 122, Form & Space: the Unity of Opposites
sources.quote: Enclose a portion of its site as an outdoor room and shelter it from undesirable climatic conditions.
sources.value: Is there a clearly enclosed outdoor room, and what does it shelter from?
sources.note: One of four site strategies (A-D) listed on the page; building-centred.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.locator: p. 122, Form & Space: the Unity of Opposites
sources.quote: Form a wall along an edge of its site and begin to define a positive outdoor space.
sources.value: Does the building edge or a boundary wall define the garden as a positive shaped space rather than leftover ground?
sources.note: Strategy A of four; uses the word positive for outdoor space.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The advantage of this type of layout is its provision of a private courtyard, sheltered by the building form and to which interior spaces can be directly related.
sources.value: Do the interior rooms open onto this sheltered private court, and which wing is communal versus private?
sources.note: Residential precedent; one wing communal, one private (same page).

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: As these openings increase in number and size, the space loses its sense of enclosure, becomes more diffuse, and begins to merge with adjacent spaces.
sources.value: Have too many or too large gaps in the boundary made the space diffuse and lost its enclosure?
sources.note: About openings in room enclosure; apply by analogy to garden gaps.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: A sunken courtyard, while protected from surface-level wind and noise by the mass surrounding it, remains a source of air, light, and views for the underground spaces opening onto it.
sources.value: Would a lowered court give shelter from wind and noise while keeping light and outlook?
sources.note: Underground-building context.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: A small opening can reveal a close-up detail or frame a view so that we see it as a painting on a wall. A long, narrow opening, whether vertical or horizontal, can not only separate two planes but also hint at what lies beyond.
sources.value: Which opening frames the view, and does its size reveal a detail, hint at more, or give the broad vista?
sources.note: Windows in rooms; transfer to gaps in garden walls and hedges.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: From within a room, a view might be tightly framed. As one moves forward, however, the view will necessarily broaden and expand until the entire view is exposed from the window sill.
sources.value: How does the framed view change as a person moves toward the opening, and where is the best standing point?
sources.note: Indoor-to-outdoor view; garden equivalent is a gap or gate.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The size and location of these openings determine, of course, the nature of the outlook as well as the degree of visual privacy for an interior space.
sources.value: Does the opening trade outlook against visual privacy deliberately?
sources.note: Interior focus.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: A group of windows can be sequenced to fragment a scene and encourage movement within a space.
sources.value: Could a series of openings reveal the garden in fragments that draw a person onward?
sources.note: Windows, not garden gaps.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: A window can be located such that a specific view can be seen from only one position in a room.
sources.value: Is there a deliberate single position from which the key view is seen?
sources.note: Interior.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: For its definition, an axis must be terminated at both of its ends by a significant form or space.
sources.value: What terminates each end of this axis, and is each end a significant form or space?
sources.note: Axis is formal; may not suit an informal garden.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Since an axis is essentially a linear condition, it has qualities of length and direction, and induces movement and promotes views along its path.
sources.value: Does the axis direct movement and views toward a destination?
sources.note: Formal organising device.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The terminating elements of an axis serve to both send and receive its visual thrust.
sources.value: What object or space receives the visual thrust at the end of the line of sight?
sources.note: The listed terminators are architectural (facades, gateways, point elements).

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Hierarchically important locations for a form or space include: • The termination of a linear sequence or axial organization • The centerpiece of a symmetrical organization • The focus of a centralized or radial organization
sources.value: Is the one most important element placed at an axis end, centre or focus?
sources.note: Bullets joined with hyphens.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Secondary points of emphasis that have less attention value than the primary focal point create visual accents.
sources.value: Is there one primary focal point with clearly subordinate accents?
sources.note: Also states over-emphasis causes confusion.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: When everything is emphasized, nothing is emphasized.
sources.value: Are too many features competing for focus?
sources.note: Short aphorism, general.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: A centralized organization is a stable, concentrated composition that consists of a number of secondary spaces grouped around a large, dominant, central space.
sources.value: Is there a dominant central space with secondary spaces grouped around it?
sources.note: Building-organisation text.

sources.document: Clark & Pause, Precedents in Architecture
sources.quote: Circulation within the central-dominant configuration is either to or around the center space. Therefore, the central space can be an outdoor space that one walks around, but generally not through.
sources.value: Do paths go to or around the central element rather than across it?
sources.note: Describes a cloister/atrium-type void.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Rhythm refers to any movement characterized by a patterned recurrence of elements or motifs at regular or irregular intervals.
sources.value: What recurs at what interval, and is the recurrence perceived?
sources.note: Architectural elements.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The movement may be of our eyes as we follow recurring elements in a composition, or of our bodies as we advance through a sequence of spaces.
sources.value: Does the repetition read both from a fixed view and while walking the sequence?
sources.note: Same page.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Elements need not be perfectly identical, however, to be grouped in a repetitive fashion. They may merely share a common trait or a common denominator, allowing each element to be individually unique, yet belong to the same family.
sources.value: Do repeated plants or features share a size, shape or detail trait so they read as one family?
sources.note: Lists size, shape and detail as the common traits.

sources.document: Clark & Pause, Precedents in Architecture
sources.quote: A field or network made from equal units in uniform relationships may be interrupted by a unique element.
sources.value: Within a repeated field (tree grid, hedge line), is there one deliberate exception that acts as accent?
sources.note: Precedent catalogue.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Since we move in Time through a Sequence of Spaces, we experience a space in relation to where we've been and where we anticipate going.
sources.value: Is the garden composed as a sequence, so each space is read against the previous and the next?
sources.note: Capitalisation as printed.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: A large space can envelop and contain a smaller space within its volume.
sources.value: Is a smaller defined space nested inside a larger one, with a clear size difference?
sources.note: Page also says the contained space must stay clearly smaller.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.locator: p. 230, Spaces Linked by a Common Space
sources.quote: Two spaces that are separated by distance can be linked or related to each other by a third, intermediate, space.
sources.value: What intermediate space links the two garden areas?
sources.note: Building-scale wording.

sources.document: Clark & Pause, Precedents in Architecture
sources.quote: Both nested and concentric patterns can be created at the formal or spatial level, and both imply layering.
sources.value: Are there successive layers, each viewed in the context of the next?
sources.note: Formal-geometry framing.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: even a change in level can establish a threshold and mark the passage from one place to another.
sources.value: Is the passage into the space marked, even subtly (level change, paired posts, beam)?
sources.note: Fragment of a longer sentence.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: the entrance into the space is best signified by establishing a real or implied plane perpendicular to the path of the approach.
sources.value: Is the entry marked by a real or implied plane across the path?
sources.note: Fragment; "exterior space" is explicitly included earlier on the page.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: A projected entrance forms a transitional space, announces its function to the approach, and provides overhead shelter. A recessed entrance also provides shelter and receives a portion of exterior space into the realm of the building.
sources.value: Is the entry projected or recessed, and does it provide a transitional space?
sources.note: Building entrances.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The form and scale of entrances and paths should also convey the functional and symbolic distinction between public promenades, private halls, and service corridors.
sources.value: Do path scale and form signal which routes are public, private or service?
sources.note: Indoor typology.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Must be segregated for privacy
sources.value: Which spaces are segregated for privacy, and from what?
sources.note: Bullet fragment in a list of program requirements; short.

sources.document: Clark & Pause, Precedents in Architecture
sources.quote: The most holy space, which is protected and separated from the outside world by a series of walls, then, is the smallest, darkest, most enclosed, and roomlike precinct in the Temple.
sources.value: Does privacy increase by stages through successive boundaries toward the most protected space?
sources.note: Sacred-temple example; the principle of graded enclosure transfers, the symbolism does not.

sources.document: Clark & Pause, Precedents in Architecture
sources.quote: Transition is the incremental change of an attribute within a finite limit.
sources.value: Does an attribute (size, openness, light) change by steps between public and private zones?
sources.note: Text lists size and open-to-closed as examples.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: This is the first phase of the circulation system, during which we are prepared to see, experience, and use the spaces within a building.
sources.value: Does the approach prepare a visitor for the destination?
sources.note: Building approach.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The approach to a building and its entrance may vary in duration from a few paces through a compressed space to a lengthy and circuitous route.
sources.value: Is the approach length and directness chosen deliberately?
sources.note: Building approach.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The continuity and scale of each path at an intersection can help us distinguish between major routes leading to major spaces and secondary paths leading to lesser spaces.
sources.value: Do path width and continuity show which route is primary?
sources.note: Same page notes pedestrians need more room than body dimensions.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: To avoid the creation of a disorienting maze, a hierarchical order among the paths and nodes of a building should be established by differentiating their scale, form, length, and placement.
sources.value: Is there a hierarchy of paths and pause points, not a maze?
sources.note: Same page: nodes give pause, rest, reorientation.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The path may pass though a space axially, obliquely, or along its edge. • In cutting through a space, the path creates patterns of rest and movement within it.
sources.value: Does the path pass by, through (axially, obliquely, along an edge) or end in each space, and what rest areas result?
sources.note: Typo "though" as printed; bullets joined by hyphen.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: The examples on the facing page illustrate how this type of spatial definition can be used to differentiate between a path of movement and places of rest
sources.value: Is the path of movement distinguished from places of rest by surface?
sources.note: Mid-sentence excerpt.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Elevating a portion of the base plane creates a specific domain within a larger spatial context.
sources.value: Does a level change carve out a distinct domain, and is its edge articulated?
sources.note: Page adds that edge treatment decides whether it reads as separate.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Be merely implied with a change in level or a contrast in surface material or texture between the two spaces.
sources.value: Can two garden areas be separated by an implied edge (level or material) rather than a wall?
sources.note: Bullet fragment (third of four ways a separating plane may act).

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: This raised space can serve as a retreat from the activity around it or be a platform for viewing the surrounding space.
sources.value: Does the raised or edge position act as a retreat and a viewing platform over the rest of the space?
sources.note: Interior room example; not about seating.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Intimate settings of tables and lounge chairs in a large hotel lobby tell us something about the expansiveness of the space as well as define comfortable, human-scale areas within it.
sources.value: Do small seating groups create human-scale pockets within a larger space?
sources.note: Hotel-lobby example.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Hot-Arid Regions Building forms should enclose courtyard spaces. • Reduce solar and conductive heat gain. • Promote cooling by evaporation using water features and plantings.
sources.value: Where water and planting are used, are they doing cooling and shading work in an enclosed court?
sources.note: Climate-driven; hot-arid regions only.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Colonnaded arbor or pergola • Promenade or allée bordered by rows of trees or hedges • Natural topographical form in the landscape
sources.value: Do rows of trees or hedges define a linear promenade space?
sources.note: The source prints allee with an accent; normalised to ASCII here.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: A bosket or grove of trees defining a shady place in a garden or park
sources.value: Does a grove of trees define a shady place in the garden?
sources.note: Caption text.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Japanese farmers coaxed pine trees to grow into tall, thick, L-shaped hedges to shield their houses and land from winter winds and snowstorms.
sources.value: Is planting used as a sheltering L-shaped screen against a named wind direction?
sources.note: Vernacular example.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: While the 12 × 16-foot room with a 9-foot ceiling might feel comfortable to most people, a 50 × 50-foot space with the same ceiling height would begin to feel oppressive.
sources.value: Is the enclosing height in proportion to the plan size so the space feels comfortable?
sources.note: Indoor figures; the original uses a multiplication sign (normalised to x).

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: While something that is monumental in scale makes us feel small in comparison, a space that is intimate in scale describes an environment in which we feel comfortable, in control, or important.
sources.value: Is this meant to be intimate or monumental in scale, and does it read so?
sources.note: Qualitative.

sources.document: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
sources.quote: Such elements as a table or chair, the risers and treads of a stairway, the sill of a window, and the lintel over a doorway, not only help us judge the size of a space but also give it a human scale.
sources.value: Which familiar-size elements (seat, step, sill) give the space a legible human scale?
sources.note: Same page cautions body dimensions vary and are not absolute.

sources.document: US DOJ, 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design
sources.locator: 303.2 Vertical, printed p.105 (Titles II and III)
sources.quote: Changes in level of ¼ inch (6.4 mm) high maximum shall be permitted to be vertical.
sources.note: Applies to: Max vertical lip/step in an accessible route (flush lid/grille/paving joints). Accessibility standard for facilities, not a hazard standard; garden routes may not be covered. Waterbody edge itself is not addressed.

sources.document: US DOJ, 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design
sources.quote: Changes in level between ¼ inch (6.4 mm) high minimum and ½ inch (13 mm) high maximum shall be beveled with a slope not steeper than 1:2.
sources.value: 6.4-13 mm bevelled at <=1:2; >13 mm must be ramped (303.4)
sources.note: Applies to: Lid or cover rim height relative to paving. Same caveat as H-ada303-vertical.

sources.document: US DOJ, 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design
sources.quote: Changes in level greater than ½ inch (13 mm) high shall be ramped, and shall comply with 405 or 406.
sources.note: Applies to: Upper limit of an un-ramped level change. Accessibility only.

sources.document: US DOJ, 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design
sources.quote: Openings in floor or ground surfaces shall not allow passage of a sphere more than ½ inch (13 mm) diameter
sources.value: 13 mm (1/2 in) max opening
sources.note: Applies to: Grating/grille aperture in a walking surface (grille over pond or fire pit). Gives a walkability limit for grates, NOT an anti-child-entrapment limit (a child body/limb entrapment check is different, none found). 1/2 in is far smaller than the 80 mm figure unverified from RoSPA.

sources.document: IES, The Lighting Handbook
sources.locator: Table 33.2 Residential Exteriors > Pool and Hot Tub Deck (printed p.33.4)
sources.quote: Pool and Hot Tub Deck LZ4i Eh @grade C 2 4 8 Avg
sources.note: Applies to: Horizontal illuminance on the deck around a pool. About swimming pool/hot tub decks (pool presumed internally lit), not a garden pond. Use as nearest analogue only.

sources.document: IES, The Lighting Handbook
sources.locator: Table 33.2 Residential Facilities Illuminance Recommendations, Residential Exteriors > Ramps, Stairs, and Steps (printed p.33.4)
sources.quote: Ramps, Stairs, and Steps LZ4i Eh @treads/landings; Ev @5' AFG C 2 4 8 Avg B 1 2 4 Avg
sources.value: LZ4: category C = 2/4/8 lx (visual ages <25 / 25-65 / >65) horizontal; lower LZ zones 0.5-1 lx
sources.note: Applies to: Illuminance at steps/level changes outdoors. Table columns are by observer age; row letters decode to the lux triples shown. Minimum maintained averages, very low values. Note beside the row: "Lighting should address the area of the steps and landings. Alternatively, draw attention to elevation changes with contrast lighting."

sources.document: IES, The Lighting Handbook
sources.quote: Reflecting pools or still-water features will simply reflect the focal light off into the direction opposite that of the incoming light. This is glary,
sources.value: qualitative: avoid external flood lighting of still water
sources.note: Applies to: Night lighting of a still koi pond. Aesthetic/glare, not a hazard figure.

sources.document: SLL, Code for Lighting
sources.locator: Table 3.5 General circulation areas at outdoor work places, 3.5.1 (printed p.96)
sources.quote: Walkways exclusively for pedestrians 5 0.25 50 20 Where there are other hazards present higher values of Ēm are required.
sources.value: 5 lx maintained, Uo 0.25
sources.note: Applies to: Outdoor pedestrian walkway minimum. Outdoor WORKPLACE table, not domestic gardens. "Other hazards" (a water body, open fire pit) imply a higher value but no figure for them is given.

sources.document: IES, The Lighting Handbook
sources.quote: Lighting key entries, site circulation routes and intersections, and elevation changes in between are important to navigating residential sites where nighttime activity is anticipated.
sources.value: qualitative
sources.note: Applies to: Light level changes of elevation on garden routes. No figure here; figures in Table 33.2.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.locator: Section 7.6 Wet Detention Ponds (Section 330), page with Figures 330-44 to 330-49
sources.quote: Safety is a concern in pond design. Slopes along the shoreline should be gradual (1:4 or less) and/or protected by dense upland plantings. A 6 000 mm (20 ft) flat shelf (1:10 slope or less) should be provided at the water's edge if possible.
sources.value: slope <= 1:4; flat shelf 6 000 mm at <= 1:10
sources.note: Applies to: Shoreline slope and safety shelf (stormwater wet ponds). About stormwater detention ponds, not a koi pond; 6 m shelf is out of scale for a garden. Printed page number not legible in OCR. OCR text has stray spaces.

sources.document: Harris & Dines, Time-Saver Standards for Landscape Architecture
sources.locator: Section 5.4 Cross-Sectional Configuration, Relationship to Plaza Level (page with Fig 530-14/15)
sources.quote: It can also serve as a barrier to prevent accidental walking or falling into the pool .
sources.value: qualitative: raised rim acts as barrier
sources.note: Applies to: Raised rim vs flush. Neutral on flush: also says an at-grade water level integrates the pool into the surrounding plane.

sources.document: Neufert, Architects' Data
sources.locator: Garden pools (page with paddling pools and irrigation; printed page not read)

rules.title: Features the brief asks for are present
rules.reference: Client brief 2026-11-22 (policy; traceability A1)
rules.fix: Add the missing feature to the plan, or record the client's waiver of it.

rules.title: Main path clear width
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-5
rules.fix: Widen the main path to 1 200 mm clear, or reclassify it as secondary if it carries one person at a time.

rules.title: Secondary path clear width (one person)
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-5
rules.fix: Widen the path to 600 mm clear (one pedestrian).

rules.title: Outdoor step riser
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-8
rules.fix: Re-divide the level change so every riser is 115-150 mm (175 mm only for a utilitarian step).

rules.title: Outdoor step relation 2R + G
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-8
rules.fix: Adjust the going so that 2 x riser + going is 650-675 mm.

rules.title: No single steps
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-8
rules.fix: Make the level change a ramp, or at least two (preferably three) steps announced by railing, planting or lighting; or remove it.

rules.title: Private stair width
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-11
rules.fix: Widen the stair to 1 050 mm.

rules.title: Rise between landings
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-11
rules.fix: Insert a landing so no flight rises more than 1 500 mm.

rules.title: Seat wall height and width
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-11
rules.fix: Bring the seat wall to 350-450 mm high and 400-450 mm wide.

rules.title: Dining zone area per seat
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 210-3, Fig. 210-3 (derived per seat)

params.basis: 4 200 mm dia. circle / 4 seats; (3.6 x 4.8 m with 1.2 m strip) / 4 seats

rules.fix: Enlarge the dining paving, or seat fewer people at it (3.46 m2 per seat; 4.32 m2 where circulation runs along one side).

rules.title: Clear strip around a dining table
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. Fig. 210-3; Time-Saver Interior 2nd ed. p. 268
rules.fix: Move the table, or the planting/wall/feature, so 1 200 mm stays clear from the table edge on all sides. Conservative: the figure shows the strip on one side only.

rules.title: Seats for the briefed group
rules.reference: Client brief 2026-11-22 (policy)
rules.fix: Add seating (a lounge group) until at least 10 people sit; standing room for the rest is a GAP.

rules.title: Clear level ground around a fire pit or BBQ
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 240-19
rules.layout: features[kind in firepit,bbq] against obstacles, buildings, planting
rules.fix: Keep 900 mm (1 200 mm recommended) of clear level hard ground on every side of the pit or BBQ stand.

rules.title: Fire ring to nearest seated person
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 520-24
rules.fix: Move the seating back to 1 500 mm from the fire, or confirm the pit is small enough for the shorter distance (the source figure is for a >= 1 800 mm ring).

rules.title: Fire pit / BBQ clearance to facade and planting declared from the product
rules.reference: Client brief 2026-11-22: product instructions
rules.fix: Enter the manufacturer's clearance for the chosen product; the check then compares it with the layout. Until then it is not_evaluated.

rules.title: Flush fire pit cover: declared load rating
rules.reference: BS EN 124 Group 1 (pedestrian areas) class A15 = 15 kN: the nearest published pedestrian-load class for a flush cover (a drainage standard, via a supplier table). No fire-pit cover standard or manufacturer walk-on figure was found
rules.fix: Specify a cover certified to at least 15 kN (EN 124 A15) by the supplier, with a heat-rated surface, or choose a design that is not walked on.

rules.title: Pond edge freeboard (water below the rim)
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 530-15
rules.fix: Lower the water level (or raise the rim) to the freeboard for the edge type.

rules.title: Flush pond: paving sloped back toward the pond
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 530-15
rules.fix: Slope the rim or the adjacent paving back toward the pond from at least 600 mm beyond the splash clearance.

rules.title: Soil depth for planting over structure
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 610-9 Table 610-4
rules.fix: Deepen the planter or raise the bed to the depth for the plant form, or change the plant form.

rules.title: Fall of paving, paths, lawn and beds
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 320-13 Table 320-2; p. 240-8
rules.fix: Re-grade: terraces 0.5-2 % (1 % preferred), walks 1-4 % cross fall, recreation lawn 1-5 %.

rules.title: One water-need class per planting group
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 750-11
rules.fix: Regroup plants so each irrigation group has one water-need class (swap species, or split the bed).

rules.title: Sense of enclosure of an outdoor room
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-4, Fig. 340-10
rules.layout: zones[use in dining,lounge,quiet].enclosure_height_m / min rect side
rules.fix: Raise the enclosing wall, screen or planting, or reduce the width of the room, until height : width reaches 1:4.

rules.title: Neighbour-side boundary height
rules.reference: Metric Handbook 7th ed. p. 22-18; client brief (privacy critical)
rules.fix: Raise the wall or fence to 1.8 m (a hedge: stated mature height and density; hedge density is a GAP).

rules.title: Mature tree root zone not covered by paving or buildings
rules.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 550-6
rules.fix: Keep paving and buildings out of the dripline, use permeable surfacing there, or move the tree.

rules.title: Service path clear width
rules.reference: Neufert 2nd English ed. 1980 p.106, Fig. 22 Dimensions of paths
rules.fix: Widen the service path to 600 mm for a wheelbarrow (900 mm for an access or garden path), or reroute.

rules.title: Lounge area per seat
rules.reference: Neufert 1980 p.211: cocktail lounge (comfortable) 1.8-2.0 m2 per person; indoor figure, borrowed
rules.fix: Enlarge the lounge zone or reduce the seats in it.

rules.title: Lounge zone holds a conversation cluster
rules.reference: Mitton & Nystuen, Residential Interior Design 4th ed. p.80: a conversation cluster is about 12-13 ft (3.66-3.96 m) across
rules.fix: Make the lounge zone at least 3.66 m across in both directions, or split it into clusters.

rules.title: Standing area per person
rules.reference: Neufert 1980 p.211: general bar (some standing, some on stools) 1.3-1.7 m2 per person; the 0.3 m2 crowd maximum of Metric Handbook Table III is NOT a comfort area
rules.fix: Enlarge the standing zone or lower the design number of standing guests.

rules.title: Tree distance to a building (zone of influence)
rules.reference: NHBC Standards 2024 ch. 4.2 Table 3b: zone of influence 1.25 / 0.75 / 0.5 x mature height (high / moderate / low water demand). UK shrinkable clay; a flag for the site soil test, not a code check
rules.fix: Move the tree, choose a species of lower water demand or lower mature height, or get the foundation depth checked by a professional.

rules.title: Hedge plant spacing within the row
rules.reference: RHS hedge planting guide: in-row planting distance 30-60 cm depending on the plants final size
rules.fix: Set the in-row planting distance to 300-600 mm to suit the species final size.

rules.title: Herb bed and fruit tree get full sun
rules.reference: RHS: full sun is more than six hours direct sun per day at midsummer; most herbs and fruit need it. Hot-desert caution: University of Arizona (afternoon shade)
rules.fix: Move the bed to a sunnier place (or accept afternoon shade deliberately for a desert site).

rules.title: Koi pond deepest section
rules.reference: Oklahoma State University Extension, Water Gardens (2017): a section at least 3-4 ft (0.9-1.2 m) deep gives fish a cool retreat
rules.fix: Deepen part of the pond to 900 mm or more (a pond supplier confirms the final depth and liner).

rules.title: Koi stocking against water surface
rules.reference: Oklahoma State University Extension, Water Gardens (2017): one 12-inch fish per 4.5 sq ft (0.42 m2) of surface unaerated; one per 2-3 sq ft aerated
rules.fix: Reduce the number of fish, enlarge the pond surface, or add aeration (a pond supplier sizes filtration).

rules.title: Plants shading the pond surface
rules.reference: Oklahoma State University Extension, Water Gardens (2017): floating or shading plants should cover 50-75 % of the pond surface
rules.fix: Plant or shade 50-75 % of the water surface (a hot site needs it for the fish).

rules.title: Fire pit or BBQ distance to structure, fence and planting
rules.reference: Calgary Fire Department: fire pits at least 2 m from house, garage or fence. Wood fuel: International Fire Code 307.4.3, 15 ft (4 572 mm). The product instructions govern (client brief)
rules.layout: features[kind=firepit|bbq] vs buildings, planting, trees, obstacles; fuel
rules.fix: Move the fire feature away from the facade and planting, or enter the product clearance (LS-FIRE-PRODUCT) and the client waives the published distance with a reason.

rules.title: Clear height above the fire
rules.reference: Manufacturer instructions: Solus 77 in (1.95 m); MAD Design 2000 mm above the flame to trees, curtains and combustible structure
rules.fix: Keep the space above the fire open to 2 m or more (no low pergola slats or tree canopy).

rules.title: Flush cover or margin: vertical lip
rules.reference: ADA Standards 2010 s.303: vertical change in level 6.4 mm (1/4 in) maximum; 6.4-13 mm bevelled; over 13 mm ramped. An accessibility standard borrowed for trip hazard
rules.fix: Set the cover flush with the paving within 6 mm, or bevel a lip up to 13 mm.

rules.title: Flush cover or grille: openings
rules.reference: ADA Standards 2010 s.302.3: openings in ground surfaces must not pass a sphere more than 13 mm (1/2 in)
rules.fix: Reduce gaps and vent slots in the cover to 13 mm across (check the product ventilation need).

rules.title: Flush pond: child protection declared
rules.reference: RoSPA: cover with a rigid metal grille; fence at least 1.1 m; Belfast Trust: fill in, else rigid grille or fence. A flush pond cannot be fenced low without contradicting the brief (concealed), so the grille is the route. No load figure is published (GAP-POND-GRILLE-LOAD)
rules.fix: Declare a rigid grille (strong enough to carry a child, secured down) just under the surface, or a fence of 1.1 m; or the client waives it with the reason.

rules.title: Flush pond: gentle shoreline
rules.reference: Time-Saver 330 s.7.6: shoreline slopes 1:4 or gentler (a stormwater-pond figure, out of scale for a koi pond); Gloucestershire FRS: gently sloping edges
rules.fix: Slope the first part of the pond floor at 1:4 or gentler (a shelf), while the koi section stays at 900 mm or more.

rules.title: Flush pond and fire pit: edge lighting at night
rules.reference: IES Lighting Handbook 10th ed. Table 33.2: pool and hot tub deck and steps, horizontal illuminance 2 / 4 / 8 lx for visual ages under 25 / 25-65 / over 65 (analogue; no figure exists for a garden pond edge)
rules.fix: Light the margin at grade to at least 4 lx (8 lx where guests are over 65) from low, shielded fixtures; do not flood the water.

advisory.title: Floor, wall and canopy make the outdoor room
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 210-2, Fig. 210-1 'Elements of spatial enclosure: floor, wall, canopy, modified by time, light, climate, and intensity of activity'
advisory.prompt: Does each outdoor room have a defined floor, walls (screen, planting) and a canopy (tree, pergola)? The numeric 1:4 limit is the quantitative rule LS-ENCLOSURE; this prompt is the qualitative side.

advisory.title: Pond edge to suit a naturalistic setting
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 530-11 (Setting) and p. 530-15 (edge conditions)
advisory.prompt: Time-Saver: a naturalistic setting directs the design toward 'organic shapes, soft edges'; an at-grade water level 'will integrate the pool into the surrounding plane'; a soft-planted edge 'is usually employed in ... naturalistic streams, ponds'. Does the pond edge match the lush tropical/Japanese character and the flush brief, and is the edge still legible as a water edge?

advisory.title: Stair rhythm suits the place
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-8, Additional Considerations 2
advisory.prompt: Is the stair's kinesthetic character congruent with the garden's character (Time-Saver: 'the sense of rhythm to be experienced by the pedestrian')?

advisory.title: Level changes announced
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 340-8, Additional Considerations 3
advisory.prompt: Is every level change, and every flush hazard edge, announced by railing, planting or lighting?
advisory.applies_to: steps, flush pond, flush fire pit

advisory.title: Lawn only where it serves a purpose
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 550-14 Practical Turf Areas
advisory.prompt: Does each lawn area have a stated purpose, a compact shape (high area-to-perimeter ratio), and no narrow strips or hard-to-irrigate slopes? (No numeric minimum width held: GAP-LAWN-WIDTH.)

advisory.title: Lush planting without heavy irrigation
advisory.reference: Time-Saver Landscape 2nd ed. p. 550-14 Planning and Design
advisory.prompt: Time-Saver: 'Xeriscape gardens do not have to be spare and bare; drought-tolerant plants can look lush without heavy irrigation.' Does the planting plan get the lush tropical/Japanese look from plants that suit the site, with irrigation concentrated where it is needed?

advisory.title: Deciduous or evergreen shade by compass side
advisory.reference: Lechner, Heating Cooling Lighting 5th ed. 2021, design guideline 'Use plants for shading'
advisory.prompt: For shade over the use areas and the facade, are trees chosen by the side they shade (true compass), noting Lechner's warning on the south side of a building? Qualitative: no shade percentage is held (GAP-SHADE-TARGET).

advisory.title: Floor, walls and canopy make an outdoor room
advisory.reference: Ching Form, Space, and Order 5th ed. pp.122, 144, 165, 17
advisory.prompt: Does each use area have a defined floor, a wall at or above eye level on at least one side, and an overhead plane (tree, pergola)? Ching: a wall along an edge begins to define a positive outdoor space; a plane near eye height begins to separate one space from another; trellis members give moderate enclosure.

advisory.title: Change of floor surface or level marks a zone
advisory.prompt: Is each zone distinguished from its neighbour by a perceptible change of surface, texture or level (rather than a drawn line)?

advisory.title: Frame the important views
advisory.reference: Ching pp.213-216
advisory.prompt: Is the pond, the best planting or the garden beyond revealed through a deliberate opening, and tighter framed from one place than another?

advisory.title: One primary focal point, with restraint
advisory.reference: Ching pp.234, 384-385, 402-403; Clark & Pause p.256
advisory.prompt: Does the gathering space have one primary focal point (the fire, a tree or a table) with lesser accents, rather than everything emphasised? Ching: when everything is emphasised, nothing is.

advisory.title: An axis ends in something worth reaching
advisory.reference: Ching p.384-385
advisory.prompt: If a path or view line is axial, is it terminated at both ends by a significant element, not left open?

advisory.title: Rhythm and repetition
advisory.reference: Ching pp.428-429; Clark & Pause p.277
advisory.prompt: Do planting, pots, stepping stones or paving joints repeat with a pattern, with one deliberate exception (Clark & Pause: a unique element interrupting a repetitive field)?

advisory.title: Layered depth and a space within a space
advisory.reference: Ching pp.224, 230, 280; Clark & Pause p.257
advisory.prompt: Does the garden read in layers (foreground, middle, background) and as a sequence of spaces, with a smaller space (quiet corner, pond) held inside a larger one?

advisory.title: Thresholds mark the change of place
advisory.reference: Ching pp.282, 290-291; Clark & Pause p.313
advisory.prompt: Is each passage between zones (house to terrace, south garden to quiet corner) marked by a threshold: a change of level or surface, a pergola or a gate-like pair of elements?

advisory.title: Graded public-to-private sequence
advisory.reference: Ching pp.232, 304; Clark & Pause p.258
advisory.prompt: Is there a graded sequence from the social space through a semi-private zone to the quiet corner, with the quiet corner reached without crossing the gathering space?

advisory.title: Paths: approach, hierarchy and relation to spaces
advisory.prompt: Does each path run to a destination, is the main route distinguishable from minor ones, and does it pass a space along its edge rather than through the middle where the space is for lingering?

advisory.title: A raised or edge retreat with a view
advisory.reference: Ching p.137
advisory.prompt: Is there a place to sit that is slightly apart or raised, with a view of the activity (Ching: a retreat from the activity or a platform for viewing)?

advisory.title: Shade tree and grove as an overhead plane
advisory.prompt: Is a shade tree or small grove used as the roof of a gathering place, with a seat beneath?

advisory.title: Human scale and intimacy
advisory.reference: Ching pp.374-375
advisory.prompt: Is each use area at a human scale: intimate settings of table and chairs inside a larger garden, not a single expansive lawn?

advisory.title: Court planting and water cool a hot dry site
advisory.reference: Ching p.57
advisory.prompt: In a hot-arid climate, do the enclosed court, planting and water work as a cooling microclimate? (Ching lists water features for evaporative cooling for hot-arid regions.)

advisory.title: Place shade trees where the afternoon sun comes from
advisory.reference: University extension / US DOE
advisory.prompt: Are deciduous or high-canopy shade trees on the east and west sides of the use area (low-branching on the west for the afternoon sun), at the distance the species allows? The figures are from US temperate climates; the latitude and Egypt orientation (LDS) decide.

advisory.title: Screen the apartment above by sight-line
advisory.reference: Washington State University Extension; University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension
advisory.prompt: Has the screen height been set by a line-of-sight from the upper window to the seating, and does an overhead canopy do the work a ground-level hedge cannot? (No published height figure for screening an upper floor exists; derive by geometry with LDS.)

advisory.title: Pond away from leaf fall, with sun but cool water
advisory.reference: OSU Extension; Neufert 1980 p.114
advisory.prompt: Is the pond clear of overhanging trees (leaf fall, roots) while its water is not in full midday sun in the hottest months? Neufert says to site pools for maximum sun, OSU warns of midday overheating: the hot site follows OSU.

advisory.title: Root barriers do not replace distance
advisory.reference: NHBC Standards 2024 ch. 4.2
advisory.prompt: If a tree is close to a building, has a professional been asked? NHBC does not accept root barriers as a substitute for the distance and foundation guidance.

advisory.title: Set a boundary hedge back from the line
advisory.reference: RHS
advisory.prompt: Is a boundary hedge set about 90 cm back from the line, and a staggered double row used where the hedge must be thicker than 90 cm?

advisory.title: Lawn in shade is mown higher
advisory.reference: RHS
advisory.prompt: Where lawn is chosen under shade, is the cutting height and mowing frequency set for shade (6 cm or more)? No source gives a minimum lawn width: that stays a gap.

advisory.title: The lid, vents and hot surface
advisory.reference: Firegear, hinged-lid gas manual, Children's Wisconsin, UC Irvine Health
advisory.prompt: Does the flush cover keep the ventilation the product needs, is below-grade installation supported by the manufacturer, can the lid be opened before ignition (interlock or sign), and is the cover marked or guarded while hot (a fire pit stays hot up to 24 h; covered coals are a hidden hazard to children)? No source gives a walk-on load or a cover surface temperature beyond EN 124 A15 (the rule); the product supplier must certify.

advisory.title: A flush edge must still read as an edge
advisory.reference: Association for Science Education SSR 247; Gloucestershire FRS; Neufert 1980; IES 26.2.4
advisory.prompt: A flush pond is concealed by the brief, yet in natural ponds grass grows over the edge and makes it very hard to see where the land ends (ASE). Is the edge marked by a contrasting margin (paving slab band, a different planting texture or deep-side planting), and not hidden by overhanging planting? Neufert wants edges concealed; the safety voices want them defined: the design must do both, and the contrast margin is a judgement (no published contrast figure exists, GAP-POND-EDGE-CONTRAST). Light the edge, not the water (IES: reflecting pools glare under flood lighting).

advisory.title: Depth that drowns a child
advisory.reference: Somerset Council (after RoSPA); Queensland QBCC; Royal Life Saving Society WA
advisory.prompt: A koi pond at 900 mm is deeper than the 300 mm at which Queensland treats a structure as a pool (ornamental fish ponds are exempt there, and RLSS WA still recommends a barrier). Somerset says a 500 mm pond is equivalent to an adult falling into 1 800 mm. Has the client been told this at the concept gate, and is a grille or protection chosen (LS-POND-GUARD)?

advisory.title: South Facing Outdoors
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 105 South Facing Outdoors; PDF pages 417-419
advisory.prompt: Is the outdoor space placed to the south of the building, with no deep band of shade between the building and the sunny part? (Latitude is a stand-in until the real site is set.)

advisory.title: Garden Growing Wild
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 172 Garden Growing Wild; PDF pages 637-638
advisory.prompt: Is any planting meant to read as a garden growing wild (intermingled, no bare earth, rough-edged boundaries) rather than a formal bed? A taste, to put to the client, not a test.

advisory.title: Still Water
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 71 Still Water; PDF pages 290-292
advisory.prompt: Where water is a still pond or pool, does a person enter it by a shallow edge that deepens gradually, rather than a sheer drop? Alexander writes this for swimming pools; here it is a prompt for the koi pond edge, to read with AD-POND-DEPTH-HAZARD.

advisory.title: Climbing Plants
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 246 Climbing Plants; PDF pages 915-916
advisory.prompt: On the sunny walls of the house or garden walls, are climbing plants trained round windows, doors, pergolas or trellises?

advisory.title: Vegetable Garden
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 177 Vegetable Garden; PDF pages 650-652
advisory.prompt: Is there a sunny, central, fenced piece of ground for growing food, with a tool store beside it? Alexander sizes this per family from a community perspective, which does not scale to one villa; use it as a prompt for the herb bed.

advisory.title: Fruit Trees
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 170 Fruit Trees; PDF pages 630-630
advisory.prompt: Are fruit trees planted as a small orchard or group that people care for and harvest, rather than as a single ornamental tree?

advisory.title: Stair Seats
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 125 Stair Seats; PDF pages 483-484
advisory.prompt: Where the garden changes level, are a few steps at the edge raised so people can sit and watch from them, immediately reachable from below?

advisory.title: Raised Flowers
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 245 Raised Flowers; PDF pages 914-915
advisory.prompt: Are flower beds raised with solid, sit-on edges beside paths, entrances and outdoor rooms, so people can touch and smell them, instead of low borders or tall tubs?

advisory.title: Paving with Cracks between the Stones
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 247 Paving with Cracks between the Stones; PDF pages 917-918
advisory.prompt: On paths and terraces, is any paving laid so grass, moss and small flowers can grow between the stones, rather than sealed concrete or mortar joints? (A finish choice for the client; the book's 1 in joint is in the card.)

advisory.title: Connection to the Earth
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 168 Connection to the Earth; PDF pages 622-623
advisory.prompt: Do paths, terraces and steps interleave the house with the earth so the boundary between building and ground is ambiguous, rather than a hard edge?

advisory.title: Site Repair
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 104 Site Repair; PDF pages 413-415
advisory.prompt: Is the building placed on the poorest part of the site, leaving the most beautiful and healthy parts (mature trees, best soil, best view) untouched? A siting prompt for the concept gate, before the garden is drawn.

advisory.title: Accessible Green
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 60 Accessible Green; PDF pages 252-256
advisory.prompt: Is there a green place to go to within a few minutes' walk of the house? In a private villa the garden itself is that green; this is a prompt, because the book's sizes are for public greens.

advisory.title: Sitting Wall
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 243 Sitting Wall; PDF pages 906-907
advisory.prompt: Are minor boundaries between outdoor areas low walls at sitting height, wide enough to sit on, rather than high fences or no boundary at all? Read with LS-SEATWALL, which carries the number.

advisory.title: Canvas Roofs
advisory.reference: Alexander, A Pattern Language, 244 Canvas Roofs; PDF pages 910-912
advisory.prompt: Where a dining or lounge space needs softer light or partial summer shade, is a folding canvas roof or awning considered, which can be opened and closed?
